::: {#exm-fdr}
#### FDR of unadjusted testing in the simulated family

In the 2000 repetitions of @exm-fwer,
average the false discovery proportion of each repetition to estimate the FDR.
The *power* of a procedure is the expected fraction of the 100 false null hypotheses it rejects, $\E{S} / m_1$:

```{r}
#| label: fdr-unadjusted
#| code-fold: false
summarize_counts <- function(counts, m1 = 100) {
  rejections <- colSums(counts[c("V", "S"), ])
  c(
    FWER = mean(counts["V", ] >= 1),
    FDR = mean(counts["V", ] / pmax(rejections, 1)),
    power = mean(counts["S", ]) / m1
  )
}
summarize_counts(sim_counts$unadjusted)
```

About `r round(100 * summarize_counts(sim_counts$unadjusted)[["FDR"]])`% of the rejections are false positives on average,
even though each individual test has only a 5% false positive rate.
A 5% rate on 900 true null hypotheses gives about `r 0.05 * 900` false positives,
which is large next to the average of `r round(mean(sim_counts$unadjusted["S", ]))` true positives.
:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

::: {#rem-fdr-fwer}
#### The FDR is never larger than the FWER

If $V \ge 1$ then $V / \max(R, 1) \le 1$ because $V \le R$,
and if $V = 0$ then $V / \max(R, 1) = 0$.
So $\text{FDP} \le \indic{V \ge 1}$,
and taking expectations gives $\text{FDR} \le \text{FWER}$.
A procedure that controls the FWER at level $\siglevel$
therefore controls the FDR at level $\siglevel$ too,
but the FDR can be controlled with many more rejections,
which is why it suits exploratory screens such as the Khan genes,
where a few false positives are an acceptable price for more discoveries.
:::
